data.title: Havránok – a Celtic cult hillfort above Liptovská Mara
data.excerpt: The hillfort of Havránok rose above Liptovská Mara, the main centre of the settlement area of the Liptov Basin, and its fortification was rebuilt three times between the Middle La Tène period and the beginning of the Roman period. On its eastern terrace stood a Celtic sanctuary with a sacrificial shaft in which the remains of at least ten sacrificed people were found, and in the time of the hillfort's greatest glory coins imitating Greek models were struck here.
data.metaTitle: Havránok at Liptovská Mara – a Celtic cult hillfort
data.metaDescription: Havránok above Liptovská Mara, a famous Celtic hillfort with a La Tène cult precinct, human sacrifices and occupation of the Púchov culture.

keyFacts.label: Location and importance
keyFacts.value: The main centre of the settlement area of the Liptov Basin, protected from the east by a landscape defensive system

keyFacts.label: Human sacrifices in the sanctuary
keyFacts.value: At least 10 sacrificed people aged 20–30, including a sixteen-year-old juvenile and a forty-year-old man

keyFacts.label: Animal offerings
keyFacts.value: Most often cattle, sheep and pigs as burnt blood offerings; occasionally also the meat of horse, dog and roe deer

keyFacts.label: Coins from Havránok
keyFacts.value: They imitated Greek coins of the Philip II of Macedon type – a boss on the obverse replacing the head, and a few dots on the horse instead of a rider

keyFacts.label: The emergency defensive wall
keyFacts.value: After the fortress was destroyed, the new north-eastern defensive wall was only 3.5 metres wide, with two rows of posts and a 90 cm wide stone face

keyFacts.label: The gate tower
keyFacts.value: A timber tower on a square plan standing on four posts; the northern wing was 260 cm high, the southern wing survived to 200 cm

keyFacts.label: Building material
keyFacts.value: Travertine blocks were brought 4 km from Bešeňová, granite stones for the roads up from the river bed over a height difference of more than 100 metres

keyFacts.label: Source of the text
keyFacts.value: Karol Pieta: Liptovská Mara. Včasnohistorické centrum severného Slovenska, Bratislava 1996

timeline.title: The oldest rampart is built
timeline.description: The oldest rampart at Havránok came into being some time during the Middle La Tène period; only its clay core, reinforced with timber grillages, has survived, recognised at only three places in the circuit mound.

timeline.year: end of the Middle La Tène period
timeline.title: The first ceremonies in the sanctuary
timeline.description: According to the oldest objects from the northern paving of the sanctuary, the first ceremonies were held here some time at the end of the Middle La Tène period.

timeline.title: Rebuilding of the hillfort
timeline.description: The hillfort was rebuilt: the western fortification, damaged by fire, was renewed and raised, and above the burnt rampart of the eastern terrace a stone wall of sandstone and travertine blocks was built; the summit plateau was fortified as well. By that time a cult precinct with a sacrificial shaft and paving already stood on the eastern terrace.

timeline.title: Third rebuilding of the fortification and enlargement of the sanctuary
timeline.description: The fortification of Havránok was rebuilt for the third time, the space of the sanctuary was enlarged and a new entrance gateway was established in the form of a timber tower on four massive posts above both wings of the defensive wall. Together with the fortification the sacrificial site was rebuilt as well; only the northern wing of the paving with its row of posts remained from the original form, and a new sacrificial shaft came into being.

timeline.year: end of the La Tène period
timeline.title: The most splendid form of the fortification
timeline.description: The fortification from the end of the La Tène period had the most splendid form – the roads were paved with granite stones brought up from the river bed, and travertine blocks from Bešeňová, 4 km away, were used in the faced masonry.

timeline.year: the hillfort's time of greatest glory
timeline.title: Coins struck at Havránok
timeline.description: According to Pavel Dvořák, coins were also struck at Havránok in the time of its greatest glory, as is proved by the discovered fragments of moulds for coin blanks; the coins imitated Greek models.

timeline.year: around the turn of the era
timeline.title: A new wall around the sacrificial site
timeline.description: Around the turn of the era a stone wall two and a half metres high grew up around the sacrificial site, and a rampart at the inaccessible places, which changed the situation of the whole sacrificial site; the old well was abolished and a new one dug.

timeline.year: end of the last century BC
timeline.title: The fortress and the sanctuary burnt down
timeline.description: The improved fortification did not withstand the enemy onslaught and the fortress was burnt down together with the sanctuary. The cult precinct of the eastern terrace came to an end at that time together with the hillfort.

timeline.year: some time after the original hillfort's demise
timeline.title: A new, reduced hillfort is built
timeline.description: The inhabitants of the settlements below the hillfort attempted to build a new hillfort on the hill, considerably reduced by the original, most accessible eastern terrace with the ruined cult place; a new north-eastern defensive wall and a new hall-type gateway with an observation platform were built.

timeline.year: at that time (after the renewal of the hillfort)
timeline.title: The first permanent occupation of the crown of the hill
timeline.description: At that time the crown of the hill was more permanently inhabited for the first time, which religious reasons had probably ruled out before; the houses were scattered or built in rows on the terraces inside the hillfort and outside it.

timeline.year: the beginning of the Roman period
timeline.title: The demise of the last fortress
timeline.description: The same places were used for the third time as fortified settlements at the beginning of the Roman period, when the fortlets and the hillforts of the Púchov culture came to a violent end at the same time. During the attack on this last fortress the gate was burnt out of the fortification, and all the houses of the settlement also fell victim to the fire.

timeline.year: second half of the 2nd century AD
timeline.title: A sporadic stay after the demise of the hillfort
timeline.description: Later the defensive walls at Havránok were never renewed again and no traces of later occupation were found either. Only in the second half of the 2nd century AD were traces recorded on the former hillfort of a sporadic stay of people who perhaps lived here briefly at the time of the exodus of the local population at the end of the Marcomannic Wars.

timeline.title: The remains of the walls as a quarry
timeline.description: The early historical fortifications at Liptovská Mara were still so distinct in the Middle Ages that they served generations of the inhabitants of the village as a quarry; parts of the walls of the eastern terrace fell victim to their efforts.

timeline.title: Celtic Day at Havránok
timeline.description: The photo gallery documents the re-enactment event Celtic Day at Havránok, held on 16 July 2011, including a staged human sacrifice in the sanctuary and a gathering of Celts.

children.text: Within the newly chosen or allotted territory the builders naturally tried to place the first houses of a new settlement so that they would best suit the economic, climatic and security factors mentioned above. Besides the communication link to the hillfort as the central point of the future area, they also had to consider the quality of the subsoil for founding houses, access to the road, to water and to land, and not least the position of the place in relation to the sun and to the direction of the prevailing winds. Earthworks followed, because apart from the land along the Váh all the other sloping positions first had to be levelled into terraces. It is therefore likely that the most advantageous places with a southern aspect were occupied first, and only after the built-up area had been enlarged also the more distant, less suitable places.

In times of acute threat the security consideration was decisive. After the first destruction of the hillfort and of part of the surrounding settlements some time at the end of the last century of the old era, the greater part of the population built their houses on narrow terraces on the top of the hill below the rampart or inside the hillfort. 
 
 
 
 
 Terraces are a typical feature of upland settlement, with particular characteristics for the building practice of the time. During long-term occupation these platforms were repeatedly cleared or enlarged by levelling, or were laid out at another place on the slope. They were exposed to erosion, and of the foundations of the original buildings only those parts have usually survived to the present day which were set towards the slope and were gradually covered by later layers or by slipped soil. At steeper places the course of the original terraces can be recognised well. Many of these artificial platforms were used as arable fields until the 1950s (until collectivisation). Because of the soil and climatic conditions most of the structures were built at ground level. Of the original dwelling or farm buildings we usually find in the field only disturbed stone footings of log walls, the remains of floors and of hearths paved with stones, and in places also the remains of charred and decayed beams. Of the post-built structures only the post holes with their stone packing have survived. Best preserved are the buildings destroyed by fire at places that were not disturbed later by building or by earthworks.
Fortification

Hillforts were a characteristic feature of the settlement structures of the northern Carpathians from the Bronze Age until the beginning of the Roman period. The early historical fortifications came into being and perished in three stages. At the end of the Early and especially during the Middle La Tène period, in the 3rd–2nd centuries BC, medium-sized but also small fortifications began to be built in new positions. Places with the remains of older Hallstatt ramparts were used only rarely. From the end of that period the characteristic “village” fortlets with a strikingly small area were built as typical defensive structures of the peripheral parts of the settlement areas, in the centre of which larger hillforts with extensive surrounding settlements dominated. The same places were used for the third time as fortified settlements at the beginning of the Roman period, when the fortlets and the hillforts of the Púchov culture came to a violent end at the same time. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 The building techniques of the hillfort builders drew on the proven practice of past generations. The basis of the fortification was a rampart of timber boxes and grillages, filled and partly heaped over with stones and earth. The height, and hence also the width, of the defensive wall derived from the possibilities and from the needs of securing a particular section of the defensive line, which usually ran along the boundary between the summit plateau and the slope. At inaccessible places there often stood only a simple palisade. The log face of the defensive wall was covered by stone cladding, which sometimes took the form of massive masonry. At the top of the mound a breastwork protected the defenders, usually fixed to vertical posts in the face of the stone revetment. 
 
 
 In the later La Tène period some new elements also appear in fortification technique, probably influenced by Celtic experience. Stone walls faced on both sides were used, and complex defensive systems of gateways were built with tower superstructures and with the fortification strengthened both outside and inside the gate. Apart from Liptovská Mara, such an exceptional fortification was partly investigated during the building of the motorway at nearby Podtureň. It was linked to an extensive system of three parallel ditches which, over a length of more than 150 metres, closed off the space towards the nearest elevation. It was undoubtedly a landscape defensive system protecting the approach from the east to the settlement area of the Liptov Basin, and thus also the approach to its main centre at Liptovská Mara. 
 
 
 The oldest rampart at Havránok came into being some time during the Middle La Tène period. Its remains were recognised at only three places in the western and the eastern part of the circuit mound, beneath several later rebuildings. Only its clay core, reinforced with timber grillages, has survived. In the interior no marked traces of contemporary occupation were found, or else they had been removed by later earthworks and rebuildings. 
 Around the middle of the 2nd century BC the hillfort was rebuilt. The western fortification, damaged by fire, was renewed and raised. Above the old burnt rampart of the eastern terrace a stone wall of large sandstone and travertine blocks was built on the rock subsoil, supported on the inside by a stony mound. We are not sufficiently informed about the fortification of the steep southern slope. It seems that a simple palisade continued here from the stone walls of the eastern terrace. In front of it another timber wall or palisade was placed as an outwork. It ran along a lower, evidently artificial terrace on which lines of massive post holes have survived beneath a row of early Roman houses. We do not know the gateway of this phase. Only from the configuration of the terrain can we assume it in the disturbed ground at the northern end of the eastern terrace, there where its course came close to the steep slope of the acropolis with the later medieval fortlet. 
 
 
 During this rebuilding, or perhaps somewhat later, the summit plateau was also fortified with a ring of simpler fortification with a faced wall. This inner defensive line, with an entrance on the accessible eastern side, had been considerably disturbed by later building alterations. Traces of fire were found at all the investigated places. By that time there already stood on the eastern terrace
a cult precinct with a sacrificial shaft and paving lined with wooden posts

. 
 The fortification of Havránok was rebuilt for the third time around the middle of the 1st century BC, when the space of the sanctuary was enlarged and a new entrance gateway, rather disadvantageous for defence, was established as the approach to the sacred precinct. It took the form of a timber tower on a square plan, erected on four massive posts above both wings of the defensive wall. The northern part, with vertical posts in the face of the masonry, was found overturned into the interior of the hillfort, but its height still reached a respectable 260 cm. The southern wing, with smooth masonry strengthened by a quantity of travertine blocks, survived in its original position to a height of 200 cm thanks to a hollow in the ground and to massive fill layers, which is more than half of the assumed height of the defensive wall. An interesting new element are the walls on the inner side of the entrance. They supported the higher-lying terrace with the southern colonnade of the sacrificial site and at the same time formed a further line of defence if the enemy broke through the gate. 
 
 
 The fortification from the end of the La Tène period had the most splendid form. The roads were paved with granite stones, which were brought up from the river bed over a height difference of more than one hundred metres. A quantity of partly dressed tuff blocks from the travertines 4 km away at Bešeňová was used in the faced masonry, because they were more resistant than the weathered sandstones quarried on the spot. Beside the defensive walls there still lay the remains of the defenders' stores – round boulders and heaps of pebbles used as projectiles.
 
 
 
 The improved fortification did not withstand the enemy onslaught, during which the fortress was burnt down together with the sanctuary at the end of the last century of the old era. After some time the inhabitants of the settlements below the hillfort attempted to build a new hillfort on the hill. In planning it they considerably reduced the original enclosed area by the most accessible eastern terrace, because the destroyed cult place had probably already lost its ancient significance for the original, or perhaps already different, population. The new defensive wall ran in the north along the edge of the summit plateau and cut across the remains of the old inner fortification, which was partly dismantled on that occasion. In the west the massive body of the old rampart was used again, where it was enough to build a simple palisade on its crest. We know the construction of the emergency north-eastern defensive wall very well. It was only 3.5 metres wide and its basis was two rows of posts joined by horizontal tie-beams. The face was formed by a 90 cm wide stone wall interspersed with posts at intervals of 160 cm. On the inside it was strengthened by a log wall, and the rear side was filled by a heaped ramp. The new hall-type gateway was built in the lower part of the reduced hillfort, at the place where the terrace ends and where the sanctuary had stood before. Because of the insufficient view towards the east, the gate had an observation platform on strong, tall posts on its upper side. 
 
 
 
 
 At that time the crown of the hill was more permanently inhabited for the first time, which religious reasons had probably ruled out before. The houses were scattered or built in rows on the terraces inside the hillfort, and possibly also outside it. A dense row of houses on the platform below the southern defensive wall formed a kind of first line of fortification, as we have been able to observe at other hillforts occupied in an emergency (Podtureň-Bašta, Jasenica). During the attack on this last fortress only the gate was burnt out of the fortification, but all the houses of this settlement and their internal furnishings also fell victim to the fire. 
 
 
 
 
 
 Later the defensive walls at Havránok were never renewed again. Nor were any traces of later occupation found. Only in the second half of the 2nd century AD did we record traces of a sporadic stay of people on the former hillfort, who perhaps lived here briefly at the time of the exodus of the local population at the end of the Marcomannic Wars. 
 The early historical fortifications at Liptovská Mara were still so distinct in the Middle Ages that they served generations of the inhabitants of the village as a quarry. Parts of the walls of the eastern terrace fell victim to their efforts. Only where they had been covered by a sufficient layer of slipped or wind-blown soil did they survive until the time of the excavations. They have endured two millennia and in their present, partly reconstructed form they are a vivid example of the building skill of the ancient inhabitants of Liptov.

children.text: Houses

The experienced carpenters of the Celtic period made effective use of the natural properties of wood. In various structural contexts they used oak, beech, fir, spruce and pine posts and beams. They felled the trees, and most of the other woodworking they did with the traditional axe made of steel of excellent quality. Excellent tools were also chisels with wooden handles and spoon augers, with which above all the joining carpentry work – mortising and wedging – was done. Saws, it seems, were not used for the rougher work. For cutting, shaving and carving there were various blades, from heavy choppers to small knives. Late La Tène building already commonly used iron nails, wedges, cramps, rivets, hooks and various fittings. 
 Dwelling buildings in the mountain environment developed under the influence of the natural conditions and of social development so as to serve their purpose as well as possible: the housing and the work of family communities. Houses were built here, according to the available space, freely on the terraces or in rows densely side by side along a road, as is attested at the well-known hillfort of Tupá skala near Vyšný Kubín. They were two-roomed log buildings with a hearth in the larger living room. A similar layout, with the addition of an unheated vestibule along two sides, was also found in the Hallstatt–La Tène dwelling uncovered on one of the terraces of the hillfort of Zvon near Lazisko in Liptov. The outer walls were not of log construction but of horizontal planks set into grooves in the corner posts. 
 The oldest houses in the settlements at Mara had a similar appearance and size. A well-preserved house of this type with an enclosure and farm buildings from the settlement became the basis for the reconstruction of the farmstead in the open-air museum. On this building destroyed by fire we can study its construction and its internal furnishings in detail. The lower part of the log structure of spruce beams was protected against damp by a row of sandstone slabs laid in a wedge-like fashion. The joints between the logs were sealed with clay daub. A peculiarity are the remains of massive posts placed at the outer corners of the walls, which carried the construction of the roof; this (with the exception of the front post beneath the ridge beam) was independent of the log shell.

blocks.caption: Another view of the reconstructed dwelling
blocks.alt: Another view of the reconstructed dwelling

children.text: The interior of the house was divided by a partition into a storage part and a living part. In the chamber stood two large storage vessels and several smaller vessels, and a spindle lay there as well. In a small jug four silver temple rings had been placed, the ornaments of the lady of the house, for which she never returned. The living part, with a plastered floor, was dominated by a hearth lined with stones. Around it the work of the members of the family was concentrated, above all cooking. On the basis of the iron fragments found and of an unfinished iron brooch, archaeologists believe that one of the inhabitants was engaged (perhaps alongside other work) in the production of simple ornaments.

In later periods, under Germanic influence, smaller single-roomed buildings with a six-post roof construction appear. We do not know whether these were farm installations, as is attested at some West Germanic settlements with large dwelling houses, or whether these small huts had a universal use in the Central European environment.

Farm buildings were undoubtedly structures with posts carrying the roof and with simple walls of poles and wattle, roughly plastered with clay mixed with chaff. Granaries – as in other regions and cultures as well – may be seen in some square ground plans with posts at the corners. Exceptionally, for example at settlement II, scattered remains of grain were even found in them. Pits, probably serving as cellars, are rare, and a single semi-sunken building was also uncovered, with a pair of posts for a tent-like roof construction.

Only two wells were found, perhaps because several springs rose on the settlements even then and a river flowed nearby. According to the pottery found, the well-preserved well at the northern foot of Havránok belonged to the earlier phase of occupation. In its upper part the walls were lined with dry-laid sandstones.
The sanctuary

The find of the remains of a Celtic sanctuary is undoubtedly an exceptional discovery from the hillfort at Havránok. According to the oldest objects from the northern paving of the sanctuary, the first ceremonies were held here some time at the end of the Middle La Tène period. On large hearths in the central part of the area sacrificial gifts were burnt; together with the remains of the pyre they were deposited in an arc-shaped band beside wooden posts (perhaps some kind of totems or stelae) running from the north towards the east. Smaller fires burnt on this area as well. From time to time the ash from the pyre deposits was covered with flat stones, and in this way a continuous paving came into being. In the centre of the precinct a pit cut into the rock was found. On its bottom lay a massive storage vessel and beside it a small jug. Around it, but also in the higher layers of the fill, incomplete skeletons as well as separate skulls and bones of several human individuals had been thrown. Beside the sacrificial pit the remains of an exceptionally large wooden post were uncovered, set 110 cm into the rock subsoil, as if the central symbol of the sanctuary. 
 
 In the middle of the 1st century BC the sacrificial site was rebuilt together with the surrounding fortification, only the northern wing of the paving with its row of posts remaining from the original form. In the centre a new shaft came into being, likewise with a wooden totem, to which another paving lined with posts led symmetrically from the southern part. The whole precinct was separated from the rest of the area of the hillfort by an enclosing fence, which in the zone beside the rampart at the same time formed its rear part. 
 The rebuilding evidently came about according to a plan and all at once. On the pavings, however, relatively few remains of offerings were now found. In the pit no parts of bodies were deposited, but only individual skulls and bones. The sanctuary was entered through a gate in the fortification, by a road running beneath the defensive wall of the eastern terrace. While the wall of the fortification was being uncovered, a vertically set sandstone block of square section, 185 cm high, was discovered. In the burnt deposit below the stone there were charred remains of various agricultural crops, burnt sherds and whole vessels, an iron ploughshare, a knife, arrowheads, silver coins and various bronze ornaments. The metal objects, unlike most of the finds from the sacrificial site, were neither deformed nor exposed to the heat of the pyre.

children.text: We assume that this is a local sacrificial place beside the road to the sanctuary, the stone prism-stele with a flat top possibly serving as the pedestal of a cult figure made of another material (wood?), or as a kind of “altar”, a purificatory, cleansing place before entering the cult precinct. On the basis of the remains of pyre deposits and of isolated whole bronze objects at other places of the defensive wall along the road destroyed by stone quarrying, we may assume that there were more such sacrificial places along the road to the sanctuary. It is interesting that a group of undamaged objects of a similar composition (bracelets, a ploughshare) was also found in the damaged part of the northern wing of the sanctuary. The cult precinct of the eastern terrace came to an end together with the hillfort at the end of the last century of the old era. From the description given it follows that two ceremonies essentially took place here: the burning of animals and of objects, and the killing of people. On the pyre various agricultural crops (peas, broad beans, wheat, barley and millet) were most often offered. As burnt blood offerings, attested in the finds by incompletely burnt bones, above all parts of the bodies of cattle, sheep and pigs were used. Occasionally the meat of horse, dog and roe deer was offered as well. Sherds, and more rarely whole vessels, are probably the remains of containers for foodstuffs, dishes and drinks which formed part of the offering or of its accompanying rites. The objects from the “ashy layer”, that is, from the deposits of cremated offerings, were varied. Ornaments and parts of female dress predominate among them: bracelets, torcs, brooches, parts of necklaces and of belts. Occasionally valuable bronze vessels, implements and tools (knives, a punch, a chisel, a ploughshare and a sickle) were also found. Nor are metal raw materials missing: iron cakes, a copper ingot, coils of silver wire and casting lumps of the same metal. Let us also mention the pieces of fragrant resin which even today, when lit, give off a distinct scent resembling thyme.

children.text: On the basis of the finds described we can attempt, at least in rough outline,
to reconstruct the course of the cremation ceremonial

. The objects, mostly sacks or vessels with crops, and the sacrificial animals were probably first received and ritually purified by the intermediaries of the cult (priests?). There followed the killing of the sacrificial animals and the separation of the parts intended for burning on the fire altar. The smashing of vessels and the deformation of metal ones had a similar meaning to the killing of an animal. The spirit of the object, which according to the ideas of the time dwelt in them just as it dwelt in an animal, had to be released. There followed the lighting of the offering, whose substance the flame transformed and which the rising smoke conveyed to the deity. For the cremation (perhaps according to certain customs and procedures) pine and fir wood was used, less often spruce, yew and oak. From the melted metal objects and from the strong burning of the rock subsoil a high heat of the pyre may be inferred. Some only slightly burnt objects, or ones untouched by fire – for example all the knives, the sickle, the vessels – may have been cult objects which were laid aside among the remains of the smouldering pyre after use, as were the remaining pieces of incense, which created a veil of scent during the burning.

blocks.caption: A Celtic ceremony in the sanctuary
blocks.alt: A Celtic ceremony in the sanctuary

children.text: We shall not be mistaken if, on the basis of certain indirect evidence, we admit the existence of a feast, which used to be part of the rites of most cults. According to the analyses of the burnt animal remains, only the lower parts of the limbs and the heads reached the pyre as “pars pro toto” – a symbolic representation of the whole – that is, the parts unsuitable for consumption. The meaty portions, together with other foodstuffs from among the offerings, were eaten after preparation at the sacred feast of the participants in the rites. By this (alongside the pleasant side of the matter) the circle of connection between those sacrificing and the supernatural recipient was at the same time closed through the consecrated offering. Possibly the vessels for drinking mead or beer also ended up smashed among the remains of the pyre after the drink had been poured out for the gods (libamen) and after the feast, because they were not allowed to leave the sacred space. At the end of the rite, at the end of the feast, the glowing embers were then scattered (this is attested) on a designated place of the paving between the posts. Here they gradually burnt out and were covered with stones and earth. According to the distribution and the quantity of the cremation remains, such offerings were a frequent custom. Those who came with them were probably individual petitioners or groups of supplicants asking for a particular favour from the all-powerful deities, or participants in thanksgiving festivals in their honour. In an attempt to continue this theoretical interpretation, we may see behind the various gifts the representatives of the individual social groups of this religious community: farmers offering their crops, craftsmen with symbolic products or metals, and members of the higher social stratum with valuable foreign goods.  The remains of human sacrifices, however, were also found in the sanctuary. At least 10 people aged 20–30 are attested. The remains of one skeleton belonged to a sixteen-year-old juvenile and parts of another to a forty-year-old person. In at least five cases women may be inferred, in a single case a man. The other skeletal finds could not be determined with certainty. Interesting insights were also brought by the study of the bones from a pathological point of view, which in as many as three cases confirmed marked anomalies in those sacrificed. On the femurs of the sixteen-year-old youth, or rather girl, from the older pit, chronic osteomyelitic changes (inflammation of the bone marrow) were found, which was a very serious health defect.

children.text: In the younger pit too a femur was found with a badly healed fracture, which meant a severe restriction of movement. Thirdly, among the fragments of skulls scattered over the area of the sacrificial site, a mandible was found with marked deformations after inflammatory processes, originally caused by an impacted right canine. Many of the skulls and of the bones of heads and limbs – were smashed and broken before death by blunt blows. On the joints of the femurs of one incomplete female skeleton traces of splitting, perhaps of the quartering of the trunk, are also visible. Finally, with another individual, places scorched by fire were found at two places on the skull and on the pelvic bone.  From these finds it is clear that people too were killed – sacrificed – at the cult place. Their remains bear traces of being beaten to death alive, of the quartering of bodies, and possibly also of burning by fire. Incomplete bodies, their smaller parts and individual heads and pieces of limbs were thrown into the pits and partly covered with earth. Many parts of those sacrificed are missing. The killing took place independently of the burning of the other offerings.  A human sacrifice was and always is the highest price, and it was once considered the most effective way of winning the favour of the gods. We know this from numerous ancient texts and we know it from ethnographic observations of primitive peoples as well, where the sacrifice of people was often connected with ritual cannibalism. There is likewise plenty of archaeological evidence, including in the Lusatian culture, which should be one of the ancient roots of the local component of the population of Mara. An even richer source of insights in this respect is the Celtic cultural sphere, with its many sanctuaries and examples of human offerings in them.  Many of the Celtic customs were described by Greek and Roman authors, among whom human ritual sacrifices were by then extremely rare, but were known from their own history as well. The Celts sacrificed people – captives, but also fellow citizens – in many ways and on various occasions, because centuries-old custom and the rituals of venerating the individual gods of their extensive pantheon required it so. To Esus people were hanged on trees, to Taranis, the ruler of the heavens, offerings were burnt, and to Teutates the victims were drowned in large vessels. That unwittingly recalls the large clay barrel found in the older of our sacrificial pits. The reasons for these cult murders were likewise manifold. By means of killing the future was divined, petitions and propitiatory offerings were presented, evil was driven out, periodic purification festivals were held and a good harvest was secured.  The origin of the custom of killing people for cult reasons is obscure, even if the Celtic sphere offers the most examples. In our case the victims were tortured (beaten), quartered and the remains thrown into a deep pit, which in fact symbolised the entrance to the underworld and contact with the deities of the earth, as the opposite of the heavenly cult. The subterranean powers ruled not only that other world of the dead but, paradoxically, also had a direct influence on the basis of life, the yield of the fields.  We come still closer to the interpretation of our find by using ethnographic descriptions of Indian harvest festivals, where the sacrifice of a human being strikingly recalls the observations from the sacrificial site at Mara. The victim's limbs were broken through and the victim was cruelly tortured, because tears, sweat and blood represented the future rain. After the killing, the flesh and parts of the victim's limbs were carried off to the fields and to the granaries, while the remains of the body were burnt or buried at the place of the rite. The motif of the harvest (the spring festivals of the first ploughing) is also indicated by the finds of ploughshares, of a sickle and by the quantity of field crops used in the sanctuary. It is to a certain extent natural that for the “scapegoat”, which carried the evil away from the community and brought the blessing of the harvest, (also) inferior, strange beings were chosen, such as perhaps the physically handicapped people from the sacrificial site.      Pavel Dvořák writes about another interesting feature of this hillfort: “True, it was not only the sacrificial site that stood at Havránok; the defensive walls encircled an extensive space with a quantity of various features, and on the meadow below them there were several relatively large unfortified villages. In the time of its greatest glory coins were also struck at Havránok, as is proved by the discovered fragments of moulds for coin blanks.       All the coins have a horse on one side and a shell-like boss on the other.

children.text: It is a remarkable testimony to traditions which people kept even when they no longer knew what they actually meant. The coins from Havránok in fact imitate Greek coins; they have their shape and their weight, and to a certain extent also their striking. The boss on the obverse replaces the head of Philip II of Macedon, who meant nothing any more to the Púchov Celts, and evidently for the same reason they turned the original rider into a little horse with a few dots on its back instead of a man in the saddle. The smoke that rose from the sanctuary at Havránok was a reminder for many centuries that the will of the gods is the highest law. Many centuries, however, are too many; in such a great span of time all sorts of things happened that changed the sanctuary from its foundations. Around the turn of the era a stone wall two and a half metres high grew up around the sacrificial site, and a rampart at the inaccessible places. The wall changed the situation of the whole sacrificial site. The old well was abolished and a new one dug. Archaeologists found only two skeletons in it, female again. The other sacrificial objects also decreased in number, and moreover they are less perfect than the offerings of the first period. Several circumstances testify to decline. It is not impossible that someone pushed the people of Havránok away from the source of raw materials. In the end catastrophe came as well. The sanctuary and the surrounding villages suddenly perished, Havránok and two of the six settlements in the neighbourhood certainly by violence. This is proved by the toppled walls and by the arrowheads stuck into the outer side of the rampart, but also by the destroyed pottery kiln in one of the settlements, a kiln from which, instead of the potter, it was only archaeologists who took out the wares two thousand years later. The fighting was hard; the high walls, the complicated fortification and the ingenious watchtower did not help the defenders. Someone was not afraid of the gods of Havránok and destroyed their temple without hesitation. Foreign people invaded the country. They burnt and devastated not only Liptovská Mara but other hillforts as well. At least seven fortifications that archaeologists have investigated in the area of Žilina, Orava, Liptov and Spiš suddenly came to an end: there remained only the defensive walls and the houses destroyed by fire, from which the people had had no time to carry out their property.”
